direct_claims: The chart displays the annual female death rate per 1,000 people of a given age across six specific age groups: 0, 10, 25, 45, 65, and 80 years old, spanning the years 1933 to 2023.
derived_claims: The chart is produced by the publication Our World in Data.
The chart compares four geographic entities: the World, India, the United States, and Japan.
The data is sourced from the Human Mortality Database (2025) and the UN World Population Prospects (2024).
The data reveals a classic U-shaped mortality curve, where death rates are highest at the extremes of life—infancy (0 years) and old age (80 years)—and lowest during childhood and young adulthood.
Japan's trajectory is particularly remarkable; starting with high mortality rates in the post-WWII era, it rapidly declined to achieve some of the lowest female mortality rates globally.
Conversely, while India has made monumental progress—reducing infant mortality from over 150 per 1,000 in the 1950s to around 25 per 1,000 in 2023—it still lags behind the US and Japan.
The sudden spike in older age mortality during 2020–2021 serves as a stark reminder of how infectious disease outbreaks can abruptly disrupt long-term health progress.
speculative_claims: In demography, measuring death rates per 1,000 people of a specific age group allows for standardized comparisons across countries with vastly different population sizes and age structures.
A notable global anomaly is the spike around 1959–1961 in the "World" series, most visible in the 10-year-old panel, which historically aligns with the Great Chinese Famine.
Additionally, a sharp spike in mortality is visible in 2020–2021, particularly in the 65 and 80 years old panels, which represents the global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The consistent downward trend in female mortality across all age groups and regions over the 90-year period represents one of humanity's greatest achievements, driven by improvements in clean water, sanitation, antibiotics, vaccines, and maternal care.
